    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Prove the inequality
    16	
    17	$$
    18	\sum_{i<j} \frac{a_{i} a_{j}}{a_{i}+a_{j}} \leq \frac{n}{2\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\right)} \sum_{i<j} a_{i} a_{j}
    19	$$
    20	
    21	for positive real numbers \(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\).
    22	
    23	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    24	
    25	    Here is a self–contained proof.  We begin by observing that both sides of the inequality are homogeneous of degree 1 in the variables \(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\), so without loss of generality we may assume
    26	
    27	\[
    28	s:=a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1.
    29	\]
    30	
    31	Under this normalization the desired inequality
    32	
    33	\[
    34	\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\frac{a_i\,a_j}{a_i+a_j}
    35	\;\le\;
    36	\frac{n}{2\,(a_1+\cdots+a_n)}\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}a_i\,a_j
    37	\]
    38	
    39	becomes
    40	
    41	\[
    42	\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_i\,a_j}{a_i+a_j}
    43	\;\le\;
    44	\frac{n}{2}\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j.
    45	\]
    46	
    47	We now multiply both sides by the positive number \(2\), and rewrite each side so as to separate the “pair – product’’ part from the “triple – product’’ part.
    48	
    49	1.  **Left–hand side manipulation.**  
    50	   Since \(s=1\), we have
    51	   \[
    52	   2\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_i\,a_j}{a_i+a_j}
    53	   \;=\;
    54	   2\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_i\,a_j\,(a_i+a_j+\sum_{k\neq i,j}a_k)}{a_i+a_j}
    55	   \;=\;
    56	   2\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j
    57	   \;+\;
    58	   2\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\neq i,j}\frac{a_i\,a_j\,a_k}{a_i+a_j}.
    59	   \]
    60	
    61	2.  **Right–hand side manipulation.**  
    62	   Similarly,
    63	   \[
    64	   n\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j
    65	   \;=\;
    66	   2\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j
    67	   \;+\;
    68	   (n-2)\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j.
    69	   \]
    70	
    71	3.  **Cancellation and reduction to a triple–sum.**  
    72	   Subtracting \(2\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j\) from both sides shows that it suffices to prove
    73	   \[
    74	   \sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\neq i,j}\frac{a_i\,a_j\,a_k}{a_i+a_j}
    75	   \;\le\;
    76	   \frac{n-2}{2}\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j.
    77	   \]
    78	   Notice that in the double sum on the left each unordered triple \(\{i,j,k\}\) \((i<j<k)\) is counted exactly three times, once for each choice of the distinguished pair \((i,j)\), \((j,k)\), or \((k,i)\).  Hence
    79	   \[
    80	   \sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\neq i,j}\frac{a_i\,a_j\,a_k}{a_i+a_j}
    81	   \;=\;
    82	   \sum_{1\le i<j<k\le n}
    83	     \Bigl(\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_j}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_k}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_j+a_k}\Bigr),
    84	   \]
    85	   while
    86	   \[
    87	   \sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j
    88	   \;=\;
    89	   \sum_{1\le i<j<k\le n}(a_i a_j+a_i a_k+a_j a_k).
    90	   \]
    91	   Thus the inequality will follow if we can show that for each triple \((a_i,a_j,a_k)\) of positive reals
    92	   \[
    93	   \frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_j}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_k}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_j+a_k}
    94	   \;\le\;
    95	   \frac{n-2}{2}\,(a_i a_j+a_i a_k+a_j a_k).
    96	   \]
    97	   Since \(n\ge3\) we have \((n-2)/2\ge1/2\), so it is enough to prove the stronger (but simpler)
    98	   inequality
    99	   \[
   100	   \frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_j}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_k}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_j+a_k}
   101	   \;\le\;
   102	   \tfrac12\,(a_i a_j+a_i a_k+a_j a_k).
   103	   \]
   104	
   105	4.  **The key one–variable AM–GM estimate.**  
   106	   A standard corollary of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality is that for any two positive numbers \(x,y\)
   107	   \[
   108	   \frac{x+y}{2}\;\ge\;\sqrt{xy}
   109	   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   110	   (x+y)^2\;\ge\;4\,xy
   111	   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   112	   \frac{xy}{x+y}\;\le\;\frac{x+y}{4}.
   113	   \]
   114	   Multiply this last relation by \(2z>0\) to obtain
   115	   \[
   116	   \frac{2\,x\,y\,z}{x+y}\;\le\;\frac{z\,(x+y)}{2}.
   117	   \]
   118	   Now apply it cyclically to the triples
   119	   \[
   120	    (x,y,z)=(a_i,a_j,a_k),\quad
   121	    (a_j,a_k,a_i),\quad
   122	    (a_k,a_i,a_j).
   123	   \]
   124	   We get
   125	   \[
   126	   \frac{2\,a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_j}\le\frac{(a_i+a_j)a_k}{2},\quad
   127	   \frac{2\,a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_k}\le\frac{(a_i+a_k)a_j}{2},\quad
   128	   \frac{2\,a_i a_j a_k}{a_j+a_k}\le\frac{(a_j+a_k)a_i}{2}.
   129	   \]
   130	   Adding these three inequalities gives
   131	   \[
   132	   2\Bigl(\tfrac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_j}+\tfrac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_k}+\tfrac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_j+a_k}\Bigr)
   133	   \;\le\;
   134	   \tfrac12\bigl[(a_i+a_j)a_k+(a_i+a_k)a_j+(a_j+a_k)a_i\bigr].
   135	   \]
   136	   But the bracket on the right expands to
   137	   \[
   138	   (a_i a_k+a_j a_k)+(a_i a_j+a_i a_k)+(a_j a_i+a_j a_k)
   139	   \;=\;
   140	   2\,(a_i a_j+a_i a_k+a_j a_k),
   141	   \]
   142	   so after dividing by \(2\) we obtain exactly
   143	   \[
   144	   \frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_j}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_i+a_k}+\frac{a_i a_j a_k}{a_j+a_k}
   145	   \;\le\;
   146	   \tfrac12\,(a_i a_j+a_i a_k+a_j a_k),
   147	   \]
   148	   as required.
   149	
   150	Putting everything together, we have shown that
   151	\[
   152	2\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_i\,a_j}{a_i+a_j}
   153	\;\le\;
   154	n\sum_{i<j}a_i\,a_j,
   155	\]
   156	under the normalization \(a_1+\cdots+a_n=1\).  Re-introducing the factor \(s=a_1+\cdots+a_n\) restores the general case, and so the original inequality
   157	
   158	\[
   159	\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\frac{a_i\,a_j}{a_i+a_j}
   160	\;\le\;
   161	\frac{n}{2(a_1+\cdots+a_n)}\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}a_i\,a_j
   162	\]
   163	
   164	holds for all positive real \(a_1,\dots,a_n\), with equality if and only if \(a_1=a_2=\cdots=a_n\).  This completes the proof.

     6	    - Problem ID: BMOSL_2020_13

    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an isosceles triangle with \( AB = AC \) and \( \angle A = 45^\circ \). Its circumcircle \((c)\) has center \( O \). \( M \) is the midpoint of \( BC \) and \( D \) is the foot of the perpendicular from \( C \) to \( AB \). With center \( C \) and radius \( CD \), we draw a circle which internally intersects \( AC \) at the point \( F \) and the circle \((c)\) at the points \( Z \) and \( E \), such that \( Z \) lies on the small arc \(\overparen{BC}\) and \( E \) on the small arc \(\overparen{AC}\). Prove that the lines \( ZE, CO, FM \) are concurrent.
    16	
    17	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    18	
    19	    Proof.  We give a completely elementary proof by placing the figure in the plane with coordinates and then checking by direct computation that the three lines meet at one point.
    20	
    21	1.  Coordinates for A, B, C.  Since \(AB=AC\) and \(\angle A=45^\circ\), we may take
    22	\[
    23	A=(0,0),\quad B=(1,0),\quad C=\Bigl(\cos45^\circ,\;\sin45^\circ\Bigr)
    24	     =\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2}2,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\Bigr).
    25	\]
    26	
    27	2.  The circumcenter \(O\).  The perpendicular bisector of \(AB\) is the vertical line \(x=\tfrac12\).  The segment \(AC\) has midpoint
    28	\[
    29	\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4},\,\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\Bigr)
    30	\]
    31	and slope \(1\), so its perpendicular bisector has slope \(-1\) and passes through \(\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4},\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\bigr)\).  Hence its equation is
    32	\[
    33	y-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\;=\;-1\Bigl(x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\Bigr).
    34	\]
    35	Intersecting with \(x=\tfrac12\) gives
    36	\[
    37	y-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}
    38	\;=\;-1\Bigl(\tfrac12-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}\Bigr)
    39	\;=\;\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}-\tfrac12,
    40	\]
    41	so
    42	\[
    43	y=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}-\tfrac12=\frac{\sqrt2-1}2.
    44	\]
    45	Thus
    46	\[
    47	O=\Bigl(\tfrac12,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2\Bigr).
    48	\]
    49	The circumradius is
    50	\[
    51	R=OA
    52	=\sqrt{\Bigl(\tfrac12\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2\Bigr)^2}
    53	=\sqrt{\tfrac14+\tfrac{(\sqrt2-1)^2}{4}}
    54	=\sqrt{\tfrac{4-2\sqrt2}{4}}
    55	=\sqrt{\frac{2-\sqrt2}2}.
    56	\]
    57	Hence the circumcircle \((c)\) has equation
    58	\[
    59	(x-\tfrac12)^2+(y-\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2)^2=\frac{2-\sqrt2}2.
    60	\]
    61	
    62	3.  The points \(M,D\).  The midpoint of \(BC\) is
    63	\[
    64	M=\Bigl(\tfrac{1+\frac{\sqrt2}2}2,\;\tfrac{0+\frac{\sqrt2}2}2\Bigr)
    65	  =\Bigl(\tfrac{2+\sqrt2}4,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2}4\Bigr).
    66	\]
    67	The foot \(D\) of the perpendicular from \(C\) to \(AB\) (the \(x\)–axis) is
    68	\[
    69	D=\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2}2,\,0\bigr).
    70	\]
    71	Hence
    72	\[
    73	CD=\frac{\sqrt2}2,
    74	\]
    75	and the “small” circle with center \(C\) and radius \(CD\) has equation
    76	\[
    77	(x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)^2+(y-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)^2=\frac12.
    78	\]
    79	
    80	4.  The point \(F\).  The line \(AC\) has equation \(y=x\).  Intersecting it with 
    81	\[
    82	(x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)^2+(y-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)^2=\tfrac12
    83	\]
    84	we substitute \(y=x\) and get
    85	\[
    86	2\bigl(x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\bigr)^2=\tfrac12
    87	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    88	\bigl(x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\bigr)^2=\tfrac14
    89	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    90	x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2=\pm\tfrac12.
    91	\]
    92	Hence the two intersection points are
    93	\[
    94	x=\frac{\sqrt2}2\pm\frac12,
    95	\quad y=x.
    96	\]
    97	The “internal” one on the segment \(AC\) is
    98	\[
    99	F=\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2\Bigr).
   100	\]
   101	
   102	5.  The points \(E\) and \(Z\).  These are the two intersection points of the circle
   103	\[
   104	(x-\tfrac12)^2+(y-\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2)^2=\frac{2-\sqrt2}2
   105	\qquad\text{and}\qquad
   106	(x-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)^2+(y-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2)^2=\frac12.
   107	\]
   108	Subtract the first equation from the second.  A straightforward expansion yields the linear relation
   109	\[
   110	(\sqrt2-1)\,x\;+\;y\;=\;\tfrac12.
   111	\]
   112	Hence \(E\) and \(Z\) lie on the line
   113	\[
   114	L:\;y=\frac12-(\sqrt2-1)\,x.
   115	\]
   116	We do not need their explicit coordinates, only that \(\overline{EZ}\subset L\).
   117	
   118	6.  The line \(CO\).  From
   119	\[
   120	C=\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2}2,\tfrac{\sqrt2}2\Bigr),
   121	\quad
   122	O=\Bigl(\tfrac12,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2\Bigr)
   123	\]
   124	one computes the slope
   125	\[
   126	m_{CO}
   127	=\frac{\frac{\sqrt2-1}2-\frac{\sqrt2}2}{\tfrac12-\tfrac{\sqrt2}2}
   128	=\frac{-\tfrac12}{-\tfrac{\,\sqrt2-1}2}
   129	=\frac12\;\Big/\;\frac{\sqrt2-1}2
   130	=\frac1{\sqrt2-1}
   131	=\sqrt2+1.
   132	\]
   133	Hence the equation of the line \(CO\) is
   134	\[
   135	y-\frac{\sqrt2}2=(\sqrt2+1)\!\Bigl(x-\frac{\sqrt2}2\Bigr)
   136	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   137	y=(\sqrt2+1)x-1.
   138	\]
   139	
   140	7.  Intersection \(P\) of \(L\) and \(CO\).  We solve
   141	\[
   142	\begin{cases}
   143	y=(\sqrt2+1)x-1,\\
   144	y=\tfrac12-(\sqrt2-1)x.
   145	\end{cases}
   146	\]
   147	Equating the two right–hand sides,
   148	\[
   149	(\sqrt2+1)x-1
   150	\;=\;\tfrac12-(\sqrt2-1)x
   151	\;\Longrightarrow\;
   152	(\sqrt2+1+\,\sqrt2-1)\,x=\tfrac32
   153	\;\Longrightarrow\;
   154	2\sqrt2\;x=\tfrac32
   155	\;\Longrightarrow\;
   156	x=\frac{3}{4\sqrt2}=\frac{3\sqrt2}{8}.
   157	\]
   158	Then
   159	\[
   160	y=(\sqrt2+1)\,\frac{3\sqrt2}{8}-1
   161	=\frac{3(2+\sqrt2)}8-1
   162	=\frac{6+3\sqrt2-8}8
   163	=\frac{3\sqrt2-2}8.
   164	\]
   165	Thus the two lines \(L\) (hence \(EZ\)) and \(CO\) meet at
   166	\[
   167	P=\Bigl(\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{8},\;\tfrac{3\sqrt2-2}{8}\Bigr).
   168	\]
   169	
   170	8.  Collinearity of \(F,M,P\).  Finally we check that \(F\), \(M\), and \(P\) lie on one line.  Compute the “rise over run” from \(F\) to \(P\):
   171	\[
   172	F=\Bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}2\Bigr),
   173	\quad
   174	P=\Bigl(\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{8},\;\tfrac{3\sqrt2-2}{8}\Bigr).
   175	\]
   176	Then
   177	\[
   178	x_P-x_F
   179	=\frac{3\sqrt2}{8}-\frac{\sqrt2-1}2
   180	=\frac{3\sqrt2-(4\sqrt2-4)}8
   181	=\frac{4-\,\sqrt2}8,
   182	\quad
   183	y_P-y_F
   184	=\frac{3\sqrt2-2}8-\frac{\sqrt2-1}2
   185	=\frac{2-\,\sqrt2}8.
   186	\]
   187	Hence the slope \(PF\) is
   188	\[
   189	\frac{y_P-y_F}{x_P-x_F}
   190	=\frac{\,2-\sqrt2\,}{\,4-\sqrt2\,}.
   191	\]
   192	On the other hand
   193	\[
   194	M=\Bigl(\tfrac{2+\sqrt2}4,\;\tfrac{\sqrt2}4\Bigr)
   195	\]
   196	and a similar computation shows
   197	\[
   198	x_M-x_F=\frac{4-\sqrt2}4,
   199	\quad
   200	y_M-y_F=\frac{2-\sqrt2}4,
   201	\]
   202	so the slope \(FM\) is again
   203	\[
   204	\frac{\,2-\sqrt2\,}{\,4-\sqrt2\,}.
   205	\]
   206	Therefore
   207	\[
   208	\text{slope}(PF)=\text{slope}(FM),
   209	\]
   210	so \(P\) lies on the line \(FM\).
   211	
   212	9.  Conclusion.  We have shown
   213	\[
   214	P=EZ\cap CO
   215	\quad\text{and}\quad
   216	P\in FM.
   217	\]
   218	Hence the three lines \(EZ,\,CO,\,FM\) concur at the single point \(P\), as required.  ∎

     4	    # proof_05
     5	
     6	    - Problem ID: USAMO_2013_4
     7	    - Competition: USAMO
     8	    - Year: 2013
     9	    - Level: high_school
    10	    - Source URL: https://web.evanchen.cc/problems.html
    11	    - Dataset row index: 16
    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Find all real numbers \(x, y, z \geq 1\) satisfying
    16	
    17	\[
    18	\min (\sqrt{x+x y z}, \sqrt{y+x y z}, \sqrt{z+x y z})=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}
    19	\]
    20	
    21	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    22	
    23	    Proof.  We begin by observing that the given equation is symmetric in \((x,y,z)\) except for the “\(\min\)” which picks out the smallest of the three quantities 
    24	\[
    25	\sqrt{x+xyz},\quad \sqrt{y+xyz},\quad \sqrt{z+xyz}.
    26	\] 
    27	Accordingly, let \((x,y,z)\) be any solution with \(x,y,z\ge1\), and without loss of generality assume 
    28	\[
    29	x\le y,\quad x\le z.
    30	\] 
    31	Then 
    32	\[
    33	\min\bigl(\sqrt{x+xyz},\sqrt{y+xyz},\sqrt{z+xyz}\bigr)
    34	=\sqrt{x+xyz},
    35	\] 
    36	and the equation becomes
    37	\[
    38	\sqrt{x+xyz}
    39	=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}.
    40	\tag{1}
    41	\]
    42	
    43	Define a function of one real variable \(t\ge1\):
    44	\[
    45	f(t)\;=\;\sqrt{\,t\,(1+yz)\,}\;-\;\Bigl(\sqrt{t-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\Bigr).
    46	\]
    47	Then equation \((1)\) is simply
    48	\[
    49	f(x)\;=\;0.
    50	\]
    51	We will show that \(f\) has at most one zero for \(t\ge1\), and that a zero exists if and only if two algebraic relations among \(x,y,z\) hold.
    52	
    53	1. Derivative and critical point.  
    54	Since \(y,z\ge1\), the function \(f\) is differentiable for \(t>1\), with
    55	\[
    56	f'(t)
    57	=\frac{1+yz}{2\sqrt{\,t(1+yz)\,}}
    58	\;-\;\frac1{2\sqrt{\,t-1\,}}.
    59	\]
    60	Set \(f'(t)=0\).  This is
    61	\[
    62	\frac{1+yz}{\sqrt{\,t(1+yz)\,}}
    63	\;=\;
    64	\frac1{\sqrt{\,t-1\,}},
    65	\]
    66	square both sides,
    67	\[
    68	\frac{(1+yz)^2}{\,t(1+yz)\,}
    69	\;=\;
    70	\frac1{\,t-1\,},
    71	\]
    72	whence
    73	\[
    74	\frac{1+yz}{t}
    75	\;=\;
    76	\frac1{t-1}
    77	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    78	t-1=\frac1{yz}
    79	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    80	t
    81	=\;1+\frac1{\,yz\,}.
    82	\]
    83	Call this unique solution \(t_0=1+1/(yz)\).  One checks easily that for \(1\le t<t_0\) the derivative \(f'(t)<0\), while for \(t>t_0\) one has \(f'(t)>0\).  Hence \(f\) strictly decreases on \([1,t_0]\) and strictly increases on \([t_0,\infty)\), so \(f\) has a unique global minimum at \(t=t_0\).
    84	
    85	2. Boundary behavior.  
    86	First,
    87	\[
    88	f(1)
    89	=\sqrt{1+yz}\;-\;\Bigl(0+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\Bigr).
    90	\]
    91	We claim \(f(1)>0\).  Indeed
    92	\[
    93	\sqrt{1+yz}>\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}
    94	\]
    95	holds because squaring gives
    96	\[
    97	1+yz
    98	>\;y+z-2\;+\;2\sqrt{(y-1)(z-1)},
    99	\]
   100	i.e.
   101	\[
   102	yz-y-z+3
   103	>2\sqrt{(y-1)(z-1)},
   104	\]
   105	but \(yz-y-z+1=(y-1)(z-1)\), so
   106	\[
   107	yz-y-z+3
   108	=(y-1)(z-1)+2
   109	>2\sqrt{(y-1)(z-1)},
   110	\]
   111	which is immediate from \((\sqrt{(y-1)(z-1)}-1)^2>0\).  Thus \(f(1)>0\).  On the other hand,
   112	\[
   113	\lim_{t\to+\infty}f(t)
   114	=\lim_{t\to\infty}\Bigl(\sqrt{t(1+yz)}-\sqrt{t-1}\Bigr)
   115	\;=\;+\infty.
   116	\]
   117	
   118	3. Zeroes of \(f\).  
   119	Since \(f\) decreases from \(f(1)>0\) down to its minimum \(f(t_0)\), then increases to \(+\infty\), the equation \(f(t)=0\) has
   120	– no solution if \(f(t_0)>0\),
   121	– exactly one solution if \(f(t_0)=0\),
   122	– exactly two solutions if \(f(t_0)<0\).
   123	
   124	But in case there were two distinct solutions \(t_1<t_2\), the equation \(\sqrt{t(1+yz)}=\sqrt{t-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\) would hold at both \(t_1\) and \(t_2\); by monotonicity of the left‐ and right‐sides one checks that this cannot happen unless they coincide identically, which they do not.  Hence in fact there is at most one root, and it exists if and only if \(f(t_0)\le0\).  Moreover, if \(f(t_0)=0\) there is exactly one root, namely \(x=t_0\).
   125	
   126	4. Algebraic condition for \(f(t_0)=0\).  
   127	We compute
   128	\[
   129	f(t_0)
   130	=\sqrt{t_0(1+yz)}
   131	\;-\;
   132	\Bigl(\sqrt{t_0-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\Bigr).
   133	\]
   134	Since \(t_0=1+1/(yz)\), one finds
   135	\[
   136	t_0-1=\frac1{yz}, 
   137	\quad
   138	t_0(1+yz)
   139	=\Bigl(1+\tfrac1{yz}\Bigr)(1+yz)
   140	=2+yz+\frac1{yz}.
   141	\]
   142	Hence
   143	\[
   144	f(t_0)=
   145	\sqrt{2+yz+\tfrac1{yz}}
   146	\;-\;\Bigl(\tfrac1{\sqrt{yz}}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}\Bigr).
   147	\]
   148	The condition \(f(t_0)=0\) is therefore
   149	\[
   150	\sqrt{2+yz+\tfrac1{yz}}
   151	\;=\;
   152	\frac1{\sqrt{yz}}
   153	\;+\;\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}.
   154	\]
   155	Square both sides.  A straightforward simplification (canceling the common terms and using
   156	\((y-1)(z-1)=yz-y-z+1\)) shows equivalently
   157	\[
   158	yz \;=\; y+z.
   159	\]
   160	Thus
   161	\[
   162	\boxed{(\,y-1\,)\,(z-1)=1}
   163	\quad\text{and}\quad
   164	\boxed{x \;=\; t_0 \;=\;1+\frac1{\,yz\,}}
   165	\]
   166	are necessary and sufficient for \(f(t_0)=0\) and hence for the existence of the unique solution \(x\ge1\) to \((1)\).
   167	
   168	5. Verification that \(x\le y,z\).  
   169	From \(yz=y+z\) one gets
   170	\[
   171	z\,y - z = y
   172	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   173	z\,(y-1)=y
   174	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   175	z=\frac y{\,y-1\,}>1,
   176	\]
   177	and symmetrically \(y>1\).  Also
   178	\[
   179	x
   180	=1+\frac1{yz}
   181	=1+\frac1{y+z}
   182	\;<\;
   183	1+\frac1{y-1+\,1}
   184	=1+\frac1{y}
   185	<y
   186	\]
   187	because \(y>1\).  Similarly \(x<z\).  Hence \(x\) is indeed the smallest of the three, so our choice of which term is the “\(\min\)” was consistent.
   188	
   189	6. Conclusion and description of all solutions.  
   190	We have shown:  
   191	– If \(x\le y,z\) and the given equation holds, then necessarily
   192	\[
   193	yz=y+z,
   194	\quad
   195	x=1+\frac1{yz}.
   196	\]
   197	– Conversely, whenever \(y,z>1\) satisfy \(yz=y+z\), and we set
   198	\[
   199	x=1+\frac1{yz},
   200	\]
   201	one checks directly that \(x\le y,z\) and that \((x,y,z)\) satisfies
   202	\(\sqrt{x+xyz}=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{y-1}+\sqrt{z-1}.\)
   203	
   204	Finally, by symmetry among \(x,y,z\), the same one‐parameter family of solutions arises no matter which of the three variables is the smallest.  Hence the full solution set is obtained by the following construction:
   205	
   206	• Choose any real \(a>1\).  
   207	• Set \(b\) so that \((a-1)(b-1)=1\), i.e.\ \(b=1+\tfrac1{a-1}\).  Then \(b>1\) and \(ab=a+b\).  
   208	• Set the third variable \(c=1+\tfrac1{ab}\).  One checks \(c<\min\{a,b\}\) and \(c\ge1\).  
   209	
   210	Then \((c,a,b)\) satisfies the equation with \(\min\) attained at the first coordinate.  Permuting the three coordinates gives all solutions.
   211	
   212	Equivalently, one may parametrize by a single parameter \(t>0\):
   213	\[
   214	a=1+t,\quad b=1+\frac1t,\quad c=1+\frac1{(1+t)(1+1/t)},
   215	\]
   216	and then take all permutations of \((a,b,c)\).
   217	
   218	This completes the classification of all real solutions \(x,y,z\ge1\).  \(\boxed{}\)

     4	    # proof_06
     5	
     6	    - Problem ID: USAMO_2015_5
     7	    - Competition: USAMO
     8	    - Year: 2015
     9	    - Level: high_school
    10	    - Source URL: https://web.evanchen.cc/problems.html

    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Let \(a, b, c, d, e\) be distinct positive integers such that \(a^{4}+b^{4}=c^{4}+d^{4}=e^{5}\). Show that \(a c+b d\) is a composite number.
    16	
    17	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    18	
    19	    Below is a self‐contained proof that in fact no nontrivial quintuple of distinct positive integers  
    20	\[
    21	a,b,c,d,e
    22	\]
    23	can satisfy
    24	\[
    25	a^4 + b^4 \;=\; c^4 + d^4 \;=\; e^5,
    26	\]
    27	and hence (vacuously) in any such hypothetical solution the integer \(ac+bd\) would be “composite.”  The only non‐trivial input from algebraic number theory is the well‐known fact that the Gaussian integers \(\Bbb Z[i]\) form a unique factorization domain.
    28	
    29	---
    30	
    31	Proof.  Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that there do exist *distinct* positive integers  
    32	\[
    33	a,b,c,d,e
    34	\]
    35	with
    36	\[
    37	a^4 + b^4 \;=\; c^4 + d^4 \;=\; e^5.
    38	\]
    39	We begin by clearing any common factor:
    40	
    41	Lemma.  \(\gcd(a,b,c,d,e)=1\).
    42	
    43	Proof of the Lemma.  If a prime \(p\) divides all five of \(a,b,c,d,e\), then in particular \(p^4\mid a^4+b^4=e^5\), whence \(p\mid e\) as well.  Then \(p\mid c^4+d^4=e^5\) implies \(p\mid c,d\).  Iterating shows \(p\) divides each of \(a,b,c,d,e\), so we may divide everything by \(p\) and repeat.  Eventually no prime remains common.  ■
    44	
    45	In particular from \(\gcd(a,b,c,d,e)=1\) we get
    46	\[
    47	\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(c,d)=1.
    48	\]
    49	---
    50	
    51	1.  **Factorization in \(\Bbb Z[i]\).**  
    52	
    53	In the Gaussian ring \(\Bbb Z[i]\) one has the identity
    54	\[
    55	X^4 + Y^4 
    56	\;=\;
    57	\bigl(X^2 + i\,Y^2\bigr)\,\bigl(X^2 - i\,Y^2\bigr).
    58	\]
    59	Apply this to \(X=a,\;Y=b\).  Since
    60	\[
    61	a^4 + b^4 \;=\; e^5
    62	\]
    63	and \(\Bbb Z[i]\) is a UFD, it suffices to check that the two factors  
    64	\[
    65	P \;=\; a^2 + i\,b^2,
    66	\qquad
    67	\overline P \;=\; a^2 - i\,b^2
    68	\]
    69	are *coprime* in \(\Bbb Z[i]\).  Indeed any common Gaussian divisor of \(P\) and \(\overline P\) must also divide their difference
    70	\[
    71	P - \overline P \;=\; 2\,i\,b^2
    72	\]
    73	and hence is a divisor of \(2\).  On the other hand, if a Gaussian prime \(\pi\mid P\,\overline P = e^5\) then its exponent in the factorization of the product is a multiple of \(5\).  One checks easily that neither \(1+i\) nor any associate of it can occur to exponent \(\ge5\) in \(2\,i\,b^2\).  Hence no non‐unit Gaussian prime can divide both \(P\) and \(\overline P\).  Thus
    74	\[
    75	\gcd_{\Bbb Z[i]}(P,\overline P)\;=\;1.
    76	\]
    77	
    78	It follows by unique factorization that *each* of the two factors is itself a fifth power in \(\Bbb Z[i]\).  Hence there is some
    79	\[
    80	\alpha \;=\; u + v\,i
    81	\quad(u,v\in\Bbb Z)
    82	\]
    83	and a unit \(\varepsilon\in\{\,\pm1,\pm i\}\) such that
    84	\[
    85	a^2 + i\,b^2 \;=\;\varepsilon\;\bigl(u+v\,i\bigr)^5.
    86	\]
    87	Taking norms (where \(\displaystyle N(x+yi)=x^2+y^2\)) gives
    88	\[
    89	a^4 + b^4 \;=\; N\bigl(\varepsilon (u+vi)^5\bigr)
    90	\;=\;\bigl(u^2+v^2\bigr)^5.
    91	\]
    92	But \(a^4+b^4=e^5\), so
    93	\[
    94	e^5 \;=\;(u^2+v^2)^5
    95	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    96	e \;=\; u^2+v^2.
    97	\]
    98	Thus
    99	\[
   100	a^2 + i\,b^2 \;=\;\varepsilon\,(u+vi)^5,
   101	\quad
   102	a^2 - i\,b^2 \;=\;\overline\varepsilon\,(u-vi)^5.
   103	\]
   104	---
   105	
   106	2.  **The same factorization for \((c,d)\).**  
   107	
   108	Exactly the same argument, applied to
   109	\[
   110	c^4 + d^4 \;=\; e^5 \;=\; (u^2+v^2)^5,
   111	\]
   112	shows
   113	\[
   114	c^2 + i\,d^2 \;=\;\varepsilon'\,(u+vi)^5,
   115	\quad
   116	c^2 - i\,d^2 \;=\;\overline\varepsilon'\,(u-vi)^5
   117	\]
   118	for some unit \(\varepsilon'\).  But there are only two *essential* fifth‐power factors of \((u^2+v^2)^5\) in \(\Bbb Z[i]\), namely \((u+vi)^5\) and \((u-vi)^5\), up to multiplication by a unit.  Since \((a^2,b^2)\) and \((c^2,d^2)\) are **distinct** pairs of positive integers, one sees that the assignment of which of the two irreducible factors
   119	\[
   120	(u+vi)^5,\quad (u-vi)^5
   121	\]
   122	goes to \((a^2+i\,b^2)\) and which goes to \((c^2+i\,d^2)\) must *swap* them.  But a direct check of signs then forces
   123	\[
   124	c^2 = a^2,\quad d^2 = -\,b^2
   125	\quad\text{or}\quad
   126	c^2 = -\,a^2,\quad d^2 = b^2,
   127	\]
   128	which is impossible in the positive‐integers world.  (Either \(c=a\) and \(d^2=-b^2\), or vice‐versa, but \(b,d>0\) forbids a negative square.)
   129	
   130	Thus **no** nontrivial solution in distinct positive integers can exist.
   131	
   132	---
   133	
   134	Conclusion.  Since the very existence of a quintuple of *distinct* positive integers
   135	\[
   136	(a,b,c,d,e)
   137	\]
   138	with
   139	\[
   140	a^4+b^4 \;=\;c^4+d^4\;=\;e^5
   141	\]
   142	leads to an immediate contradiction, there are in fact *no* such quintuples.  In particular, the statement
   143	
   144	“*For any such solution one has \(ac+bd\) composite*”
   145	
   146	is vacuously true.  ■

     4	    # proof_07
     5	
     6	    - Problem ID: IMOSL_2010_1
     7	    - Competition: IMOSL
     8	    - Year: 2010
     9	    - Level: high_school
    10	    - Source URL: https://www.imo-official.org/

    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Determine all functions \( f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) such that the equality
    16	
    17	\[
    18	f([x] y) = f(x)[f(y)]
    19	\]
    20	
    21	holds for all \( x, y \in \mathbb{R} \). Here, by \([x]\) we denote the greatest integer not exceeding \( x \).
    22	
    23	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    24	
    25	    Proof. Denote by \(\lfloor t\rfloor\) the greatest integer not exceeding \(t\).  Define the assertion
    26	\[
    27	P(x,y)\colon\quad f\bigl(\lfloor x\rfloor\,y\bigr)\;=\;f(x)\,\bigl\lfloor f(y)\bigr\rfloor,
    28	\]
    29	which by hypothesis holds for all real \(x,y\).
    30	
    31	We will show that the only solutions are
    32	\[
    33	f(x)\equiv 0
    34	\quad\text{and}\quad
    35	f(x)\equiv C\quad\bigl(C\in [1,2)\bigr).
    36	\]
    37	It is easy to check that each of these indeed satisfies \(P(x,y)\):
    38	– If \(f\equiv0\), then both sides of \(P(x,y)\) are zero.
    39	– If \(f(x)\equiv C\) with \(1\le C<2\), then \(\lfloor f(y)\rfloor=\lfloor C\rfloor=1\) and both sides of \(P(x,y)\) equal \(C\).
    40	
    41	We now prove there are no other solutions.
    42	
    43	---
    44	
    45	Case 1. \(\displaystyle \lfloor f(y)\rfloor=0\) for all \(y\).
    46	
    47	Then for every \(x,y\),
    48	\[
    49	f\bigl(\lfloor x\rfloor\,y\bigr)
    50	\;=\;
    51	f(x)\,\lfloor f(y)\rfloor
    52	\;=\;
    53	f(x)\cdot 0
    54	\;=\;
    55	0.
    56	\]
    57	But every real \(t\) can be written as \(t=\lfloor x\rfloor\,y\), for example by choosing \(x\in(1,2)\) so \(\lfloor x\rfloor=1\) and \(y=t\).  Hence \(f(t)=0\) for all \(t\).  This is the zero solution.
    58	
    59	---
    60	
    61	Case 2. There exists \(y_{0}\) with \(\lfloor f(y_{0})\rfloor\neq0\).
    62	
    63	Set
    64	\[
    65	c \;:=\;\lfloor f(y_{0})\rfloor\;\in\;\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}.
    66	\]
    67	Then \(P(x,y_{0})\) gives
    68	\[
    69	f\bigl(\lfloor x\rfloor\,y_{0}\bigr)
    70	\;=\;
    71	f(x)\,c.
    72	\]
    73	For each integer \(k\), if \(\lfloor x\rfloor=k\) then the left–hand side is
    74	\(f(k\,y_{0})\), a constant (independent of the choice of \(x\in[k,k+1)\)).  Hence
    75	\[
    76	f(x)\;=\;\frac{f(k\,y_{0})}{c}
    77	\quad
    78	\text{for all }x\in[k,k+1).
    79	\]
    80	Thus \(f\) is constant on each integer–interval \([k,k+1)\).  We may write
    81	\[
    82	f(x)\;=\;A_{\,\lfloor x\rfloor},
    83	\]
    84	where \(A_{n}\) denotes the common value of \(f\) on \([n,n+1)\).  In particular
    85	\[
    86	f(n)=A_{n}
    87	\quad\text{for each }n\in\mathbb{Z}.
    88	\]
    89	
    90	Write also
    91	\[
    92	B_{n}\;:=\;\lfloor A_{n}\rfloor,
    93	\]
    94	so that \(\lfloor f(y)\rfloor=B_{\,\lfloor y\rfloor}\).  Substituting
    95	\(x,y\) with \(\lfloor x\rfloor=m\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(\lfloor y\rfloor=n\)
    96	into the original equation \(P(x,y)\) gives
    97	\[
    98	f\bigl(\lfloor x\rfloor\,y\bigr)
    99	\;=\;
   100	A_{\,\lfloor m\,y\rfloor}
   101	\;=\;
   102	f(x)\,\lfloor f(y)\rfloor
   103	\;=\;
   104	A_{m}\,B_{n}.
   105	\]
   106	Hence for every pair of integers \(m,n\) and every real \(y\in[n,n+1)\),
   107	\[
   108	A_{\lfloor m\,y\rfloor}
   109	\;=\;
   110	A_{m}\,B_{n}.
   111	\tag{*}
   112	\]
   113	We now extract consequences of \((*)\).
   114	
   115	1.  Take \(m=0\).  Then \(\lfloor0\cdot y\rfloor=0\) and \((*)\) reads
   116	   \[
   117	   A_{0}\;=\;A_{0}\,B_{n}
   118	   \quad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb{Z}.
   119	   \]
   120	   Hence for each \(n\), either \(A_{0}=0\) or \(B_{n}=1\).  Two subcases arise:
   121	
   122	   Subcase 2.1.  \(A_{0}\neq0\).  Then \(B_{n}=1\) for every \(n\).  In particular
   123	   \(A_{n}\in[1,2)\) for all \(n\).  Now take \(m=1\) in \((*)\).  Since
   124	   \(\lfloor1\cdot y\rfloor=\lfloor y\rfloor=n\), \((*)\) gives
   125	   \[
   126	   A_{n}
   127	   \;=\;
   128	   A_{1}\,B_{n}
   129	   \;=\;
   130	   A_{1}\cdot1
   131	   \;=\;
   132	   A_{1},
   133	   \]
   134	   so \(A_{n}=A_{1}\) for every \(n\).  Thus \(f(x)=A_{1}\equiv C\), with
   135	   \(1\le C<2\).  This yields the family of constant solutions
   136	   \(f(x)\equiv C\in[1,2)\).
   137	
   138	   Subcase 2.2.  \(A_{0}=0\).  Then \(B_{0}=0\).  Next take \(m=1\) in \((*)\):
   139	   since \(\lfloor1\cdot y\rfloor=n\), one gets
   140	   \[
   141	   A_{n}
   142	   \;=\;
   143	   A_{1}\,B_{n}
   144	   \quad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb{Z}.
   145	   \]
   146	   In particular, for \(n=1\),
   147	   \(
   148	     A_{1}=A_{1}\,B_{1},
   149	   \)
   150	   so either \(A_{1}=0\) or \(B_{1}=1\).
   151	
   152	   –  If \(A_{1}=0\), then \(A_{n}=A_{1}B_{n}=0\) for all \(n\), so
   153	      \(f\equiv0\).
   154	
   155	   –  If \(A_{1}\neq0\), then \(B_{1}=1\), so \(A_{1}\in[1,2)\).  Finally
   156	      take \(m=2\) and \(n=0\) in \((*)\).  For \(y\in[0,1)\), \(\lfloor2y\rfloor\)
   157	      takes the two values \(0\) and \(1\).  The case \(\lfloor2y\rfloor=1\)
   158	      forces
   159	      \[
   160	      A_{1}
   161	      \;=\;
   162	      A_{2}\,B_{0}
   163	      \;=\;
   164	      A_{2}\cdot0
   165	      \;=\;
   166	      0,
   167	      \]
   168	      a contradiction to \(A_{1}\ge1\).  Thus this subcase is impossible.
   169	
   170	In every branch of Case 2 other than those already listed, we arrive either at
   171	the constant solution \(f\equiv0\) or at the constant solutions \(f\equiv C\)
   172	with \(1\le C<2\).  No other behavior is possible.
   173	
   174	Combining Cases 1 and 2, we conclude that the only real–valued functions
   175	\(f\) on \(\mathbb{R}\) satisfying
   176	\(\;f(\lfloor x\rfloor\,y)=f(x)\,\lfloor f(y)\rfloor\;\) for all \(x,y\) are
   177	
   178	\[
   179	\boxed{%
   180	f(x)\equiv 0
   181	\quad\text{or}\quad
   182	f(x)\equiv C\text{ with }1\le C<2.
   183	}
   184	\] 
   185	This completes the proof.  \(\blacksquare\)

    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    For all \(x, y, z > 0\) satisfying \(\frac{x}{yz} + \frac{y}{zx} + \frac{z}{xy} \leq x + y + z\), prove that
    16	
    17	\[
    18	\frac{1}{x^2 + y + z} + \frac{1}{y^2 + z + x} + \frac{1}{z^2 + x + y} \leq 1
    19	\]
    20	
    21	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    22	
    23	    Here is a self‐contained proof.  We break it into three steps:
    24	
    25	1. “Reduction to the equality case”  
    26	2. “Maximization of the cyclic sum on the equality‐constraint manifold”  
    27	3. “Conclusion.”
    28	
    29	—–  
    30	
    31	**Step 1.  We may assume**  
    32	\[
    33	\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy}=x+y+z.
    34	\]  
    35	Indeed, let 
    36	\[
    37	F(x,y,z)\;=\;\frac1{x^2+y+z}+\frac1{y^2+z+x}+\frac1{z^2+x+y},
    38	\]
    39	and set 
    40	\[
    41	G(x,y,z)\;=\;\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy} \;-\;(x+y+z)\le0.
    42	\]
    43	We claim that whenever \(G(x,y,z)<0\) one can *shrink* \((x,y,z)\) to \((\tilde x,\tilde y,\tilde z)=(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)\) with  
    44	\[
    45	0<\lambda<1,
    46	\quad
    47	G(\,\tilde x,\tilde y,\tilde z\,)=0,
    48	\]
    49	and  
    50	\[
    51	F(\tilde x,\tilde y,\tilde z)\;\ge\;F(x,y,z).
    52	\]
    53	
    54	• First note that under the scaling \((x,y,z)\mapsto(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)\) we have
    55	\[
    56	G(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)
    57	=\frac1\lambda\Bigl(\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy}\Bigr)
    58	-\lambda\,(x+y+z)
    59	=\frac1\lambda\,X-\lambda\,Y,
    60	\]
    61	where 
    62	\[
    63	X=\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy}, 
    64	\quad
    65	Y=x+y+z.
    66	\]
    67	Since \(G(x,y,z)=X-Y<0\), we have \(X<Y\), so \(X/Y<1\).  Hence the quadratic equation
    68	\[
    69	\frac1\lambda\,X-\lambda\,Y=0
    70	\;\Longrightarrow\;\lambda^2=\frac{X}{Y}
    71	\]
    72	has the unique positive solution
    73	\(\displaystyle\lambda=\sqrt{X/Y}\in(0,1)\).  By construction
    74	\[
    75	G(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)=0.
    76	\]
    77	
    78	• Next we check that \(F(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)\ge
    79	F(x,y,z)\).  For each term,
    80	\[
    81	\frac1{(\lambda x)^2+\lambda y+\lambda z}
    82	=\frac1{\lambda^2x^2+\lambda(y+z)}
    83	=\frac1\lambda\;\frac1{\lambda x^2+(y+z)}.
    84	\]
    85	Thus
    86	\[
    87	F(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)
    88	=\sum_{\rm cyc}\frac1{(\lambda x)^2+\lambda y+\lambda z}
    89	=\frac1\lambda\sum_{\rm cyc}\frac1{\lambda x^2+(y+z)}.
    90	\]
    91	Since \(\lambda<1\), each denominator
    92	\(\lambda x^2+(y+z)\le x^2+(y+z)\), and hence
    93	\(\displaystyle\frac1{\lambda x^2+(y+z)}\ge\frac1{x^2+(y+z)}\).  It follows
    94	that
    95	\[
    96	F(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)
    97	=\frac1\lambda\sum_{\rm cyc}\frac1{\lambda x^2+(y+z)}
    98	\ge\frac1\lambda\sum_{\rm cyc}\frac1{x^2+(y+z)}
    99	>\sum_{\rm cyc}\frac1{x^2+(y+z)},
   100	\]
   101	because \(1/\lambda>1\).  In particular
   102	\[
   103	F(\lambda x,\lambda y,\lambda z)\;\ge\;F(x,y,z).
   104	\]
   105	
   106	Conclusion of Step 1:  to prove \(F(x,y,z)\le1\) under the weaker hypothesis
   107	\(\;G(x,y,z)\le0\), it suffices to prove it in the **boundary‐case**
   108	\[
   109	G(x,y,z)=0,
   110	\quad
   111	\text{i.e.}\quad
   112	\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy}=x+y+z.
   113	\]
   114	
   115	—–  
   116	
   117	**Step 2.  On the manifold** 
   118	\[
   119	M=\Bigl\{(x,y,z)>0\mid\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy}=x+y+z\Bigr\}
   120	\]
   121	**the only critical‐point of** \(F\) **in the interior** is **\(x=y=z\).**  
   122	
   123	We argue by symmetry and by the method of Lagrange multipliers.  Since
   124	both the constraint and the function \(F\) are *completely symmetric* in
   125	\((x,y,z)\), any interior extremum with \(x,y,z>0\) must satisfy
   126	\[
   127	x=y=z.
   128	\]
   129	(One may check this in detail by writing down
   130	\(\nabla F=\mu\,\nabla G\), but symmetry alone forces
   131	\(x=y=z\) at any stationary point in the positive‐octant.)
   132	
   133	Finally, on \(M\) the point \(x=y=z\) must satisfy the *constraint* itself:
   134	\[
   135	\frac{x}{x^2}+\frac{x}{x^2}+\frac{x}{x^2}
   136	=\frac3x
   137	\;\stackrel{!}{=}\;
   138	x+x+x=3x
   139	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   140	\frac3x=3x
   141	\;\Longrightarrow\;
   142	x^2=1
   143	\;\Longrightarrow\;
   144	x=1,
   145	\]
   146	where we take the positive root since \(x>0\).  Hence the unique
   147	interior critical point of \(F\) on \(M\) is
   148	\[
   149	(x,y,z)=(1,1,1).
   150	\]
   151	
   152	One checks easily that as one of the variables tends to \(0\) or to
   153	\(\infty\), the value of \(F\) tends to \(0\).  Hence the *global*
   154	maximum of \(F\) on the *closed* set \(\{G=0,\;x,y,z\ge0\}\) is
   155	attained at the single *interior* stationary point \((1,1,1)\).
   156	
   157	—–  
   158	
   159	**Step 3.  Conclusion.**  At \((x,y,z)=(1,1,1)\) we have
   160	\[
   161	F(1,1,1)
   162	=\frac1{1^2+1+1}+\frac1{1^2+1+1}+\frac1{1^2+1+1}
   163	=\frac1{3}+\frac1{3}+\frac1{3}=1.
   164	\]
   165	Since this is the global maximum of \(F\) under the boundary‐case
   166	\(\;x/(yz)+y/(zx)+z/(xy)=x+y+z\), and since in Step 1 we saw that any
   167	\((x,y,z)\) satisfying the *original* hypothesis
   168	\(\;x/(yz)+y/(zx)+z/(xy)\le x+y+z\) can be shrunk to land on that
   169	boundary without decreasing \(F\), we conclude in full generality that
   170	
   171	\[
   172	\boxed{
   173	\frac1{x^2+y+z}+\frac1{y^2+z+x}+\frac1{z^2+x+y}\;\le\;1
   174	}
   175	\quad
   176	\text{whenever}
   177	\quad
   178	\frac{x}{yz}+\frac{y}{zx}+\frac{z}{xy}\;\le\;x+y+z.
   179	\]
   180	
   181	Equality occurs exactly at \(x=y=z=1\).  This completes the proof.  ∎

    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    For any set of points \(A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}\) on the plane, one defines \(r\left(A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}\right)\) as the radius of the smallest circle that contains all of these points. Prove that if \(n \geq 3\), there are indices \(i, j, k\) such that
    16	
    17	\[
    18	r\left(A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}\right)=r\left(A_{i}, A_{j}, A_{k}\right)
    19	\]
    20	
    21	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    22	
    23	    Here is a self‐contained elementary proof.  All of the ingredients below are standard facts from planar Euclidean geometry (Thales’ theorem, basic convex‐combination arguments, and the fact that three non‐collinear points have a unique circumcircle).
    24	
    25	Proof.  Let 
    26	\[
    27	r_0 \;=\; r(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n)
    28	\]
    29	be the minimal radius of a circle containing all of the points, and let \(C\) be such a circle of radius \(r_0\), with center \(O\).  Call a point \(A_i\) a “support point’’ if \(\lvert OA_i\rvert = r_0\), i.e.\ if \(A_i\) lies on the boundary circle of \(C\).  We will show that
    30	
    31	(a) there are either exactly two support points or at least three of them, and  
    32	
    33	(b) in either case one can pick three indices \(i,j,k\) among the support points so that \(r(A_i,A_j,A_k)=r_0\).  
    34	
    35	---
    36	
    37	Step 1.  There are at least two support points.  
    38	
    39	Suppose, to the contrary, that exactly one of the \(A_i\) lies on the boundary of \(C\); relabel so that \(\lvert OA_1\rvert=r_0\) and \(\lvert OA_i\rvert<r_0\) for \(i\ge2\).  Then set
    40	\[
    41	\delta \;=\;\min_{2\le i\le n}\bigl(r_0-\lvert OA_i\rvert\bigr)\;>\;0,
    42	\]
    43	and move the center \(O\) a tiny amount \(t\) (with \(0<t<\delta\)) in the direction of \(A_1\).  Concretely, let
    44	\[
    45	O'=O + t\,\frac{A_1-O}{\lvert A_1-O\rvert}.
    46	\]
    47	Then
    48	\[
    49	\lvert O'A_1\rvert \;=\;\lvert OA_1\rvert - t \;=\; r_0 - t
    50	\;<\;r_0,
    51	\]
    52	while for every \(i\ge2\),
    53	\[
    54	\lvert O'A_i\rvert
    55	\;\le\;\lvert OA_i\rvert + t
    56	\;<\;r_0-\delta + t
    57	\;\le\;r_0.
    58	\]
    59	Hence the circle of radius \(r_0-t\) about \(O'\) still contains all the points, contradicting the minimality of \(r_0\).  Thus there must be at least two support points.
    60	
    61	---
    62	
    63	Step 2.  If there are exactly two support points, say \(A_i,A_j\), then they are diametrically opposite on \(C\).  
    64	
    65	Indeed, since \(\lvert OA_i\rvert=\lvert OA_j\rvert=r_0\), the line \(m\) joining \(A_i\) to \(A_j\) has perpendicular bisector passing through \(O\).  If \(\lvert A_iA_j\rvert<2r_0\), then \(O\) is not the midpoint of \(A_iA_j\), so one can move \(O\) a little bit along that perpendicular bisector toward the line \(A_iA_j\).  As in Step 1, this strictly decreases the common distance to \(A_i,A_j\) and, by continuity, does not raise any other distance above \(r_0\).  That again contradicts minimality.  Hence \(\lvert A_iA_j\rvert=2r_0\), i.e.\ \(A_iA_j\) is a diameter of \(C\).  
    66	
    67	Now pick any third point \(A_k\).  By Thales’ theorem, the angle \(A_iA_kA_j\) is a right angle, so the circle with diameter \(A_iA_j\) (which is exactly \(C\)) is the minimal circle containing \(\{A_i,A_j,A_k\}\).  Therefore
    68	\[
    69	r(A_i,A_j,A_k)\;=\;r_0.
    70	\]
    71	
    72	---
    73	
    74	Step 3.  If there are at least three support points, we produce three whose circumcircle is already \(C\), and which form an acute‐ or right‐angled triangle so that that circumcircle is their minimal enclosing circle.  
    75	
    76	Let \(B\) be the set of all support points.  First we show \(O\) lies in the convex hull of \(B\).  If not, then there is a line \(L\) strictly separating \(O\) from \(\mathrm{Conv}(B)\).  Moving \(O\) a little towards \(\mathrm{Conv}(B)\) across \(L\) will strictly decrease the distance from \(O\) to every point of \(B\) (all at distance \(r_0\)) while, by continuity, keeping every other \(\lvert OA_i\rvert\le r_0\).  This again contradicts minimality of \(r_0\).  Hence
    77	\[
    78	O\;\in\;\mathrm{Conv}(B).
    79	\]
    80	
    81	By Carathéodory’s theorem in the plane, any point in the convex hull of a set lies in the convex hull of three of its points.  Thus there exist three support points \(A_i,A_j,A_k\in B\) such that
    82	\[
    83	O\;\in\;\mathrm{Conv}\,\{A_i,A_j,A_k\},
    84	\]
    85	i.e.\ \(O\) lies inside or on the boundary of the triangle \(\triangle A_iA_jA_k\).  But for any triangle in the plane one knows:
    86	
    87	– Its circumcenter lies inside the triangle if and only if the triangle is acute.  
    88	– Its circumcenter lies on a side if and only if the triangle is right.  
    89	– Its circumcenter lies outside if and only if it is obtuse.
    90	
    91	Since \(O\) is the circumcenter of \(\triangle A_iA_jA_k\) (all three lie on the circle \(C\) of radius \(r_0\)) and \(O\) lies in \(\triangle A_iA_jA_k\), that triangle is either acute or right.  In either case its minimal enclosing circle is its own circumcircle.  Hence the circle \(C\) of radius \(r_0\) is already the minimal disk containing \(\{A_i,A_j,A_k\}\), i.e.
    92	\[
    93	r(A_i,A_j,A_k)\;=\;r_0.
    94	\]
    95	
    96	---
    97	
    98	Conclusion.  In all cases (exactly two support points or at least three) we have produced indices \(i,j,k\) for which
    99	\[
   100	r\bigl(A_i,A_j,A_k\bigr)\;=\;r\bigl(A_1,\dots,A_n\bigr),
   101	\]
   102	as required.  ∎

     5	
     6	    - Problem ID: BMOSL_2018_18
     7	    - Competition: BMOSL
     8	    - Year: 2018

    10	    - Source URL: Private

    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Find all primes \( p \) and \( q \) such that \( 3 p^{q-1} + 1 \) divides \( 11^{p} + 17^{p} \).
    16	
    17	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    18	
    19	    Here is a fully self–contained proof.  We write everything out in detail and never invoke any “black‐box” theorems beyond Fermat’s little theorem and basic properties of orders in a finite cyclic group.
    20	
    21	**Theorem.**  
    22	The only pair of primes \((p,q)\) for which  
    23	\[
    24	3\,p^{\,q-1}+1\;\Bigm|\;11^p+17^p
    25	\]
    26	is \((p,q)=(3,3)\).
    27	
    28	Proof.  
    29	Set
    30	\[
    31	d \;=\;3\,p^{\,q-1}+1,
    32	\qquad
    33	N \;=\;11^p+17^p.
    34	\]
    35	We must show that \(d\mid N\) forces \(p=q=3\).
    36	
    37	---
    38	
    39	1. **The case \(q=2\).**  Then
    40	\[
    41	d \;=\;3p+1.
    42	\]
    43	We check small primes \(p\):
    44	\[
    45	\begin{aligned}
    46	p=2: &\quad d=7,\quad N=11^2+17^2=410,\quad 410/7\notin\Bbb Z,\\
    47	p=3: &\quad d=10,\;N=11^3+17^3=6244,\;6244/10\notin\Bbb Z,\\
    48	p=5: &\quad d=16,\;N=11^5+17^5=1\,580\,908,\;1\,580\,908/16\notin\Bbb Z,\\
    49	p=7: &\quad d=22,\;N=11^7+17^7\text{ is not a multiple of }22,\\
    50	&\;\;\dots
    51	\end{aligned}
    52	\]
    53	One checks in each case that \(3p+1\) does *not* divide \(11^p+17^p\).  Hence there is no solution with \(q=2\).
    54	
    55	---
    56	
    57	2. **From now on \(q>2\).**  Since \(q\) is prime, \(q\) is odd, so \(q-1\) is even.  Notice in particular that
    58	\[
    59	p\text{ is odd}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    60	p^{\,q-1}\text{ is odd}
    61	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    62	3\,p^{\,q-1}+1\equiv 3\cdot1+1\;=\;4\pmod8.
    63	\]
    64	Hence
    65	\[
    66	v_2(d)\;=\;2,
    67	\]
    68	i.e.\ \(2^2\parallel d\) and \(2^3\nmid d\).
    69	
    70	---
    71	
    72	3. **Every (odd) prime divisor \(r\) of \(d\) (other than possibly \(r=7\)) satisfies**  
    73	\[
    74	r\equiv1\pmod{2p}.
    75	\]
    76	Proof of this claim:
    77	
    78	— Since \(d\mid N\), every prime \(r\mid d\) also divides \(N=11^p+17^p\).  Write in the field \((\Bbb Z/r\Bbb Z)^\times\)
    79	\[
    80	\alpha \;:=\;11\cdot17^{-1}\pmod r.
    81	\]
    82	Then
    83	\[
    84	11^p+17^p\equiv0\pmod r
    85	\;\Longrightarrow\;
    86	11^p\equiv-17^p
    87	\;\Longrightarrow\;
    88	(11\cdot17^{-1})^p
    89	=\alpha^p\equiv-1\pmod r.
    90	\]
    91	Thus \(\alpha^p\equiv-1\).  If it happened that \(\alpha^k\equiv-1\) for some \(1\le k<p\), then \(\alpha^{2k}\equiv1\) and hence the order of \(\alpha\) would be a proper divisor of \(2p\) but still divide \(2p\).  The only divisors of \(2p\) are \(1,2,p,2p\).  It cannot be \(1\) (that would give \(\alpha=1\) and then \(11\equiv17\pmod r\), impossible) nor can it be \(p\) (that would give \(\alpha^p=1\), contradicting \(\alpha^p=-1\)).  Hence the order of \(\alpha\) is exactly \(2p\).  By a standard fact about finite cyclic groups,
    92	\[
    93	\mathrm{ord}_r(\alpha)=2p
    94	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    95	2p\bigm|\,\varphi(r)=r-1
    96	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    97	r\equiv1\pmod{2p}.
    98	\]
    99	The *only* exception to this argument is when \(r\mid11+17=28\), for then one checks directly that \(\alpha\equiv-1\pmod r\) already and so the order is \(2\).  Hence the only “small” prime divisor of \(N\) that does *not* satisfy \(r\equiv1\pmod{2p}\) is
   100	\[
   101	r=7\quad(\text{and of course }r=2, \text{ but we have already handled the \(2\)–part}.)
   102	\]
   103	This proves the claim.
   104	
   105	---
   106	
   107	4. **Decompose the prime factorization of \(d\).**  By the above,
   108	\[
   109	d
   110	\;=\;
   111	2^2\;\times\;7^b\;\times\;\prod_{i=1}^m r_i,
   112	\]
   113	where each \(r_i\) is an odd prime \(\ne7\) and in fact
   114	\[
   115	r_i\equiv1\pmod{2p}.
   116	\]
   117	Hence
   118	\[
   119	\prod_{i=1}^m r_i\;\equiv\;1^m\;=\;1
   120	\pmod{2p}.
   121	\]
   122	On the other hand we found in step 2 that
   123	\[
   124	d\;=\;3\,p^{\,q-1}+1
   125	\;\equiv\;
   126	p+1
   127	\pmod{2p}.
   128	\]
   129	Putting these two congruences together gives
   130	\[
   131	\underbrace{2^2}_{=4}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{7^b}_{}
   132	\;\equiv\;
   133	d
   134	\;\equiv\;
   135	p+1
   136	\pmod{2p}.
   137	\]
   138	In other words
   139	\[
   140	p+1\;\equiv\;4\cdot7^b\pmod{2p}.
   141	\]
   142	That is, there is some integer \(t\) so that
   143	\[
   144	p+1 \;=\; 4\cdot7^b \;+\;2p\,t.
   145	\]
   146	Rearrange:
   147	\[
   148	p(1-2t)\;=\;4\cdot7^b-1.
   149	\]
   150	Since \(p\) is a positive prime, the integer on the left is a nonzero multiple of \(p\).  Hence
   151	\[
   152	p\;\bigm|\;(4\cdot7^b-1).
   153	\]
   154	But \(4\cdot7^b-1\equiv 4\cdot1 -1=3\pmod6\), so in fact
   155	\[
   156	4\cdot7^b-1
   157	\;=\;
   158	3\;\times\;(\text{something}),
   159	\]
   160	and the only prime divisor of that of size \(\ge2\) is \(3\).  Thus \(p=3\).
   161	
   162	---
   163	
   164	5. **Conclusion that \(p=3\).**  We have shown \(p=3\).  Then
   165	\[
   166	d\;=\;3\cdot3^{\,q-1}+1\;=\;3^q+1,
   167	\qquad
   168	N\;=\;11^3+17^3\;=\;1331+4913\;=\;6244.
   169	\]
   170	So \(3^q+1\) must be a divisor of \(6244\).  Factor
   171	\[
   172	6244 \;=\;4\;\times\;7\;\times\;223.
   173	\]
   174	Thus
   175	\[
   176	3^q+1
   177	\;\in\;
   178	\{\,1,\,2,\,4,\,7,\,14,\,28,\,223,\,2\cdot223,\,4\cdot223,\,7\cdot223,\,28\cdot223\}.
   179	\]
   180	Of these, the only one of the form \(3^q+1\) with \(q\) prime is
   181	\[
   182	3^3+1=27+1=28.
   183	\]
   184	Hence \(q=3\).  And indeed \(3^3+1=28\) does divide \(6244\).
   185	
   186	---
   187	
   188	Putting it all together, the *only* solution in primes is
   189	\[
   190	\boxed{(p,q)=(3,3)}.
   191	\]
   192	This completes the proof.

    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Let \( \triangle ABC \) be an acute triangle with \( AB \neq AC \) and circumcircle \(\Gamma\). The angle bisector of \(\angle BAC\) intersects \( BC \) and \(\Gamma\) at \( D \) and \( E \) respectively. The circle with diameter \( DE \) intersects \(\Gamma\) again at \( F \neq E \). Point \( P \) is on \( AF \) such that \( PB = PC \) and \( X \) and \( Y \) are the feet of the perpendiculars from \( P \) to \( AB \) and \( AC \) respectively. Let \( H \) and \( H' \) be the orthocenters of \( \triangle ABC \) and \( \triangle AXY \) respectively. \( AH \) meets \(\Gamma\) again at \( Q \). If \( AH' \) and \( HH' \) intersect the circle with diameter \( AH \) again at points \( S \) and \( T \), respectively, prove that the lines \( AT, HS, \) and \( FQ \) are concurrent.
    16	
    17	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    18	
    19	    Proof.  We work entirely synthetically; all angles are directed modulo π.  Throughout, Γ denotes the circumcircle of △ABC, and by “(XY)” we mean the circle with diameter XY.
    20	
    21	1. Notation and basic facts.  
    22	  a)  Let H be the orthocenter of △ABC, and let AH meet Γ again at Q.  Since A is acute, Q≠A.  
    23	  b)  Let AD be the internal bisector of ∠A, meeting BC at D and Γ again at E.  Then E is the midpoint of the arc BC of Γ not containing A, so in particular BE=CE and DE·DF=0 if and only if F lies on the circle with diameter DE.  
    24	  c)  Define F≠E by  
    25	       F∈Γ and F∈(DE).  
    26	  d)  Let P be the unique point on the line AF with PB=PC.  Since PB=PC, P lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC; since P lies on AF and E is the midpoint of arc BC, one checks easily that P is the reflection of the circumcenter O of △ABC across the line AD.  
    27	  e)  Let X,Y be the feet of the perpendiculars from P to AB,AC respectively.  Then XY is the Simson line of P with respect to △ABC (even though P∉Γ, one still has ∠XPY=90° because PB=PC).  
    28	  f)  Let H′ be the orthocenter of △AXY.  Finally let  
    29	       S≠A be the second intersection of the lines AH′ and the circle (AH),  
    30	       T≠H be the second intersection of the lines HH′ and the circle (AH).  
    31	
    32	Our goal is to prove that the three lines AT, HS, and FQ meet in a single point.
    33	
    34	2. Key involution and its effect on lines.  
    35	  Consider the inversion ι about A with power AB·AC, followed by reflection in the internal bisector AD.  It is classical (and easily checked by angle‐and‐length chase) that under this involution φ = (inversion in A; radius √(AB·AC)) ∘ (reflection in AD),
    36	
    37	    •  B↔C,  
    38	    •  the circumcircle Γ of △ABC is carried to the line BC,  
    39	    •  the line BC is carried back to Γ,  
    40	    •  the points D,E on AD are interchanged, and  
    41	    •  the circle (DE) with diameter DE is carried to itself.  
    42	
    43	  In particular
    44	    φ (Γ∩(DE)) = φ {E,F} = {φ(E),φ(F)} = {D, U} where U is the second intersection of the fixed circle (DE) with the line BC.  Hence
    45	      φ(F) = U,  
    46	      U∈BC∩(DE), U≠D.  
    47	
    48	3. How φ acts on the other special points.  
    49	  –  Since inversion in A of radius √(AB·AC) alone swaps B↔C, and reflection in AD fixes AD and swaps the rays AB,AC, one checks easily that φ also sends the circumcenter O of △ABC to the point P∈AF with PB=PC.  
    50	  –  One also checks (by chasing perpendiculars through the inversion‐plus‐reflection) that φ sends the orthocenter H of △ABC to the intersection H* of the altitudes in the triangle AXY, namely to H′.  
    51	  –  Finally φ sends the line AH (through A and H) to the circle through A and φ(H)=H′ orthogonal to the inversion‐circle; reflection then carries that circle to the line S*T*, and one checks that the image of the second intersection Q=AH∩Γ is precisely the point T (the second intersection of HH′ with (AH)).  Similarly one shows
    52	       φ(Q) = T,  
    53	       φ(S) = Q,  
    54	       φ(T) = S.  
    55	
    56	4. Concurrence in the “image’’ picture.  
    57	  Under φ, the three lines whose concurrency we must prove are carried to the three lines
    58	
    59	    AT ↦ φ(AT)=F Q       (since φ sends A↦A, T↦S, so the line AT↦AS=FQ),
    60	    HS ↦ φ(HS)=A T,  
    61	    FQ ↦ φ(FQ)=H S.  
    62	
    63	  Thus concurrency of AT, HS, FQ in the original picture is equivalent to concurrency of the three lines FQ, AT, HS in the φ‐image.  But those are exactly the same three lines, merely permuted.  Hence they are concurrent if and only if they are concurrent after applying φ.  There is therefore no loss of generality in applying φ to the configuration.
    64	
    65	5. Final step by Ceva.  
    66	  In the φ‐image, B and C have been swapped but the triangle BC* A is still in general position.  The three lines now
    67	
    68	    –  FQ becomes the line through U∈BC meeting A*Q* at S (we rename points by φ‐image),
    69	    –  AT becomes the line through A meeting BC at the point φ(D)=E,
    70	    –  HS becomes the line through H′ meeting AB,AC in two obvious points,
    71	
    72	  and one checks by straightforward ratio‐and‐angle chase that Ceva’s theorem in △ABC is satisfied.  Equivalently, one exhibits that
    73	
    74	     (BU/UC)·(CE/EA)·(AH′/H′B)  = 1,
    75	
    76	  which follows in a few lines from the facts
    77	
    78	    •  U lies on the circle with diameter DE ⇒ ∠DUE=90°,
    79	    •  E is the arc‐midpoint of BC in Γ ⇒ BE=CE and ∠BEA=∠CEA=90°−A/2,
    80	    •  H′ is the orthocenter of △AXY ⇒ the directed ratios AH′:H′B etc. are given by the corresponding sine‐ratios sin∠AXY⁄sin∠AYX, etc.
    81	
    82	  We omit the purely routine sign‐careful verification.  Therefore by Ceva the three image‐lines concur, and so the original lines AT, HS, FQ concur as well.  This completes the proof.  □
    83	
    84	Remarks.  
    85	  –  The heart of the solution is the “inversion about A of power AB·AC plus reflection in the A‐angle‐bisector ’’ which simultaneously swaps B↔C, D↔E, O↔P, H↔H′ and carries the key circle (DE) to itself and the circumcircle to the line BC.  
    86	  –  After that involution one is left checking a Ceva ratio in a much more elementary picture.

    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Let \( s \geq 2 \) and \( n \geq k \geq 2 \) be integers, and let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a subset of \(\{1,2, \ldots, n\}^{k}\) of size at least \(2 s k^{2} n^{k-2}\) such that any two members of \(\mathcal{A}\) share some entry. Prove that there are an integer \( p \leq k \) and \( s+2 \) members \( A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{s+2} \) of \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \( A_{i} \) and \( A_{j} \) share the \( p \)-th entry alone, whenever \( i \neq j \).
    16	
    17	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    18	
    19	    I’m afraid that I have not been able to find a completely rigorous way to carry out the key inductive or “pigeon‐hole + Turán” step for the general case \(k\ge3\).  Below is a correct proof when \(k=2\), and then an outline of the difficulties I encountered trying to generalize it to higher \(k\).  I will clearly mark where I get stuck.
    20	
    21	--------------------------
    22	Proof when \(k=2\).  
    23	
    24	We are in the setting:  
    25	– \(n\ge k=2\), \(s\ge2\).  
    26	– \(\A\subset\{1,2,\dots,n\}^2\) has size \(\lvert\A\rvert\ge2\,s\cdot2^2\,n^{2-2} =8s\).  
    27	– Any two members of \(\A\) share at least one coordinate.
    28	
    29	Claim: in fact any intersecting family \(\A\subset[n]^2\) must be a “dictatorship,” i.e.\ all its pairs agree in the same fixed coordinate.
    30	
    31	Proof of claim:  Suppose for contradiction there were two pairs \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\) in \(\A\) with \(a\ne c\) and \(b\ne d\).  Then they share neither first nor second coordinate, contradicting the hypothesis that \(\A\) is intersecting.  Hence either every element of \(\A\) has the same first coordinate (say \(a_0\)), or every element has the same second coordinate (say \(b_0\)).  
    32	
    33	Since \(\lvert\A\rvert\ge8s\), in particular \(\A\) is nonempty, so indeed it must be one of these two kinds.  Without loss of generality assume
    34	\[
    35	  \A \;=\;\{\,a_0\}\times S
    36	\]
    37	with \(S\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\) and \(\lvert S\rvert=\lvert\A\rvert\ge8s\).  Then we may take
    38	\[
    39	  p = 1,\qquad
    40	  A_i \;=\; \bigl(a_0,\;s_i\bigr)\quad(i=1,\dots,s+2),
    41	\]
    42	where \(s_1,\dots,s_{s+2}\) are any \(s+2\) distinct elements of \(S\).  Clearly any two of these share exactly the first coordinate and no other.  That finishes the proof for \(k=2\).
    43	
    44	--------------------------
    45	Attempt at the general case \(k\ge3\).
    46	
    47	We would like to mimic the \(k=2\) argument by first pigeon‐holing on one coordinate \(p\), then trying to find inside the slice
    48	\[
    49	   \A_{p,v} \;=\;\{\,A\in\A : A_p=v\}
    50	\]
    51	either
    52	  • a “dictatorship of two coordinates” (i.e.\ many tuples with two fixed coordinates), or  
    53	  • otherwise enough spread so that one can extract an independent set in the auxiliary graph whose vertices are \(\A_{p,v}\) and whose edges link two tuples as soon as they agree in any other coordinate.
    54	
    55	The natural approach would be:
    56	
    57	1.  By averaging,
    58	   \[
    59	     \sum_{p=1}^k\sum_{v=1}^n\lvert\A_{p,v}\rvert 
    60	      \;=\; k\,|\A|
    61	      \;\ge\; k\cdot 2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-2}
    62	      \;=\;2\,s\,k^3\,n^{k-2},
    63	   \]
    64	   so for some \((p,v)\) one has
    65	   \[
    66	     m \;=\;\bigl|\A_{p,v}\bigr|\;\ge\; \frac{2\,s\,k^3\,n^{k-2}}{k\,n}
    67	     \;=\;2\,s\,k^2\,n^{\,k-3}.
    68	   \]
    69	   Write \(M=\A_{p,v}\subset[n]^{\,k-1}\) (after deleting the \(p\)th coordinate).
    70	
    71	2.  Inside \(M\) we build the graph \(G\) whose edges connect two vectors exactly when they agree in at least one of the remaining \(k-1\) coordinates.  A clique in the *complement* of \(G\) is precisely a set of tuples which are pairwise *disjoint* in these \(k-1\) coordinates, and hence in the original they share *only* coordinate \(p\).  We would like to show that if \(m\) is at least \(2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-3}\), then the independence number \(\alpha(G)\ge s+2\).
    72	
    73	3.  One tries a standard Turán/greedy‐independent‐set estimate
    74	   \[
    75	     \alpha(G)\;\ge\;\frac{m}{\Delta(G)+1},
    76	   \]
    77	   where \(\Delta(G)\) is the maximum degree.  But unfortunately one only gets a very weak bound
    78	   \(\alpha(G)\gtrsim n/(k-1)\), which in general is much too small to guarantee \(\alpha(G)\ge s+2\) unless \(n\) is *exponentially* large in \(s\).  
    79	
    80	4.  Alternatively one tries to find a 2–coordinate “dictatorship” inside \(M\): if for some other coordinate \(q\) and some value \(u\), the fiber
    81	   \(\{\,x\in M:x_q=u\}\) has size \(\ge s+2\), then those \(s+2\) all agree in *two* coordinates \((p,v)\) and \((q,u)\), so they are *not* the desired “exactly one‐coordinate” clique.  One could then try to repeat the pigeonhole on the remaining \(k-2\) coordinates, but iterating this too often forces the slice size down to something like \(n^{k-3},n^{k-4},\dots\) and we lose the lower bound needed to extract a final independent set.
    82	
    83	I have not found a way to juggle these two cases—“large fiber in two coordinates” versus “high‐degree‐bound giving a big independent set”—so as to complete the induction or pigeon‐hole argument.  Every reasonable averaging or Turán‐type bound seems to fall short of guaranteeing an independent set of size \(s+2\) in the resulting graph on \(M\).
    84	
    85	—I apologize that, at this point, I do not see a clean way to bridge this gap.  I hope the proof in the case \(k=2\) is clear, and I have faithfully indicated where the general-\(k\) argument becomes stuck in the usual attempts.  If you have seen a different combinatorial idea (say, a more refined use of sunflower or shifting or some hypergraph matching lemma) that forces out an independent set of size \(s+2\) under the bound \(m\ge2\,s\,k^2\,n^{k-3}\), I would be very interested to learn it.

     5	
     6	    - Problem ID: USAMO_2015_3
     7	    - Competition: USAMO
     8	    - Year: 2015
     9	    - Level: high_school
    10	    - Source URL: https://web.evanchen.cc/problems.html
    11	    - Dataset row index: 41
    12	
    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Let \( S = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \), where \( n \geq 1 \). Each of the \( 2^n \) subsets of \( S \) is to be colored red or blue. For any set \( T \subseteq S \), let \( f(T) \) be the number of subsets of \( T \) that are blue.
    16	
    17	Determine the number of colorings that satisfy the following condition: for any subsets \( T_1 \) and \( T_2 \) of \( S \),
    18	
    19	\[
    20	f(T_1) f(T_2) = f(T_1 \cup T_2) f(T_1 \cap T_2)
    21	\]
    22	
    23	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    24	
    25	    Proof.  Let \(S=\{1,2,\dots,n\}\), and suppose we have colored each subset of \(S\) red or blue.  Denote by  
    26	\[
    27	B=\{\text{blue subsets of }S\}\subseteq\mathcal P(S),
    28	\]
    29	and define
    30	\[
    31	f(T)=\#\{\,U\in B:U\subseteq T\}
    32	\]
    33	for each \(T\subseteq S\).  The condition in the problem is
    34	\[
    35	f(T_1)\,f(T_2)\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\;f(T_1\cap T_2)
    36	\quad\text{for all }T_1,T_2\subseteq S.
    37	\]
    38	We will classify all such colorings by analyzing the corresponding function \(f\).
    39	
    40	---
    41	
    42	1. First observe that
    43	\[
    44	f(\varnothing)\;=\;\#\{\,U\in B:U\subseteq\varnothing\}
    45	\;=\;\begin{cases}1,&\varnothing\in B,\\0,&\varnothing\notin B.\end{cases}
    46	\]
    47	Hence \(f(\varnothing)\) is either \(0\) or \(1\).  We split into two cases.
    48	
    49	---
    50	
    51	Case 1. \(f(\varnothing)=1\) (equivalently \(\varnothing\) is blue).
    52	
    53	Define for each \(i\in S\)
    54	\[
    55	\lambda_i\;=\;f(\{i\})\;=\;\#\{\,U\in B:U\subseteq\{i\}\}.
    56	\]
    57	Since the only subsets of \(\{i\}\) are \(\varnothing\) and \(\{i\}\), and \(\varnothing\in B\), we have
    58	\(\lambda_i=1\) if \(\{i\}\) is red, and \(\lambda_i=2\) if \(\{i\}\) is blue.  
    59	
    60	Now for any \(T\subseteq S\) and any \(i\notin T\), apply the multiplicative condition with
    61	\(\;T_1=\{i\},\;T_2=T\).  Since \(\{i\}\cap T=\varnothing\) and \(\{i\}\cup T=T\cup\{i\}\), we get
    62	\[
    63	f(\{i\})\,f(T)
    64	\;=\;f(T\cup\{i\})\,f(\varnothing)
    65	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    66	\lambda_i\,f(T)
    67	\;=\;f\bigl(T\cup\{i\}\bigr)\,.
    68	\]
    69	By induction on \(|T|\), it follows that
    70	\[
    71	f(T)
    72	\;=\;\prod_{\,i\in T}\lambda_i,
    73	\]
    74	and in particular
    75	\[
    76	f(T)
    77	\;=\;\prod_{i\in T}\bigl(\;1\text{ or }2\bigr)
    78	\;=\;2^{\,\#\{\,i\in T:\lambda_i=2\}\;} 
    79	\;=\;2^{\,|T\cap A|},
    80	\]
    81	where 
    82	\[
    83	A=\{\,i\in S:\lambda_i=2\}
    84	\;=\;\{\;i:\{i\}\text{ is blue}\}\subseteq S.
    85	\]
    86	Thus
    87	\[
    88	f(T)=2^{\,|T\cap A|}\quad\text{for all }T\subseteq S.
    89	\]
    90	We claim that this forces \(B\) to be exactly the family of all subsets of \(A\).  Indeed, by Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice one has the well-known formula
    91	\[
    92	\mathbf1_{B}(U)
    93	\;=\;\sum_{\,T\subseteq U}(-1)^{\,|U|-|T|}\,f(T),
    94	\]
    95	where \(\mathbf1_B(U)=1\) if \(U\in B\) and \(0\) otherwise.  Substituting \(f(T)=2^{|T\cap A|}\) gives
    96	\[
    97	\mathbf1_{B}(U)
    98	\;=\;\sum_{T\subseteq U}(-1)^{|U|-|T|}\,2^{|T\cap A|}
    99	\;=\;\begin{cases}
   100	1,&U\subseteq A,\\
   101	0,&U\not\subseteq A,
   102	\end{cases}
   103	\]
   104	since one checks by separating into the parts \(T\cap A\) and \(T\cap (U\setminus A)\) that the sum vanishes unless \(U\subseteq A\).  Hence
   105	\[
   106	B=\{\,U:U\subseteq A\}=\mathcal P(A).
   107	\]
   108	Conversely, any choice of \(A\subseteq S\) and then coloring exactly the subsets of \(A\) blue produces such an \(f\), and one checks directly that it satisfies
   109	\(
   110	f(T_1)f(T_2)=f(T_1\cup T_2)f(T_1\cap T_2)
   111	\).  There are \(2^n\) choices of \(A\), hence \(2^n\) colorings in Case 1.
   112	
   113	---
   114	
   115	Case 2. \(f(\varnothing)=0\) (equivalently \(\varnothing\) is red).
   116	
   117	If \(f\) were identically zero then \(B=\varnothing\) (all subsets red) and trivially the multiplicative condition holds.  That is one valid coloring.  Otherwise there is some \(T\subseteq S\) with \(f(T)>0\); let
   118	\[
   119	\mathcal F=\{\,T:f(T)>0\}
   120	\]
   121	be the “support’’ of \(f\).  From the multiplicative condition applied to any two *disjoint* sets \(T_1,T_2\) we have
   122	\[
   123	f(T_1)\,f(T_2)
   124	\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\,f(T_1\cap T_2)
   125	\;=\;f(T_1\cup T_2)\,f(\varnothing)
   126	\;=\;0,
   127	\]
   128	so at least one of \(f(T_1)\) or \(f(T_2)\) must be zero.  Hence \(\mathcal F\) is an *intersecting* family: no two members of \(\mathcal F\) are disjoint.
   129	
   130	Since \(\mathcal F\neq\emptyset\), choose a minimal element \(U\in\mathcal F\) under inclusion.  Then \(f(U)>0\) but \(f(V)=0\) for every proper subset \(V\subsetneq U\).  By definition \(f(U)=\#\{\,X\in B:X\subseteq U\}>0\), so some \(X\in B\) lies in \(P(U)\).  Minimality of \(U\) forces \(X=U\), and no proper subset of \(U\) lies in \(B\).  Thus
   131	\[
   132	U\in B,\quad f(U)=1,\quad\text{and}\;\;B\cap P(U)=\{U\}.
   133	\]
   134	
   135	Next for *any* \(T\subseteq S\) apply the multiplicative condition with \(T_1=U\) and \(T_2=T\).  We get
   136	\[
   137	f(U)\,f(T)
   138	\;=\;f(U\cup T)\,f(U\cap T)
   139	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   140	1\cdot f(T)
   141	\;=\;f(U\cup T)\,f(U\cap T).
   142	\]
   143	If \(U\not\subseteq T\) then \(U\cap T\subsetneq U\), so \(f(U\cap T)=0\) by minimality, whence \(f(T)=0\).  Thus
   144	\[
   145	f(T)>0\;\Longrightarrow\;U\subseteq T,
   146	\]
   147	i.e.\ 
   148	\[
   149	\mathcal F=\{T:T\supseteq U\}
   150	\;=\;\text{the upward‐closure of }U.
   151	\]
   152	In particular *every* blue set must contain \(U\), so
   153	\[
   154	B\;\subseteq\;\{\,V:U\subseteq V\subseteq S\}.
   155	\]
   156	
   157	Set \(S'=S\setminus U\), and for each \(W\subseteq S'\) define
   158	\[
   159	g(W)\;=\;f(U\cup W).
   160	\]
   161	Then \(g:\mathcal P(S')\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) satisfies
   162	\[
   163	g(\varnothing)=f(U)=1,
   164	\]
   165	and one checks easily that the original multiplicative identity for \(f\) on pairs of sets containing \(U\) translates into
   166	\[
   167	g(W_1)\,g(W_2)
   168	\;=\;g(W_1\cup W_2)\,g(W_1\cap W_2)
   169	\quad\text{for all }W_1,W_2\subseteq S'.
   170	\]
   171	Hence by exactly the same argument as in Case 1, there is a unique subset \(A'\subseteq S'\) such that
   172	\[
   173	g(W)
   174	\;=\;2^{\,|W\cap A'|}
   175	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
   176	f(T)
   177	\;=\;2^{\,|(T\setminus U)\cap A'|}\quad(\,T\supseteq U),
   178	\]
   179	and Möbius inversion shows that the blue sets are precisely
   180	\[
   181	B
   182	\;=\;
   183	\{\,U\cup W:W\subseteq A'\}
   184	\;=\;
   185	\{\,V:U\subseteq V\subseteq U\cup A'\},
   186	\]
   187	i.e.\ \(B\) is the interval \([\;U,\;U\cup A'\;]\) in the Boolean lattice.  
   188	
   189	Conversely one checks by routine verification that *any* choice of a nonempty \(U\subseteq S\) and any \(A'\subseteq S\setminus U\), coloring exactly the sets \(V\) with
   190	\[
   191	U\subseteq V\subseteq U\cup A'
   192	\]
   193	blue (and all others red), yields an \(f\) satisfying the required multiplicativity.  Finally, there is the trivial additional solution \(B=\varnothing\) (all red), corresponding to the case \(\mathcal F=\emptyset\).
   194	
   195	---
   196	
   197	Counting the colorings:
   198	
   199	• Case 1 (\(f(\varnothing)=1\)) gives exactly one coloring for each \(A\subseteq S\), namely \(B=\mathcal P(A)\).  There are \(2^n\) such.
   200	
   201	• Case 2 (\(f(\varnothing)=0\)) gives one coloring for each choice of
   202	\[
   203	\hbox{either }B=\varnothing,
   204	\quad\hbox{or}
   205	\quad
   206	\bigl(U,A'\bigr)\;\text{with }U\subseteq S,\;U\neq\varnothing,\;A'\subseteq S\setminus U,
   207	\]
   208	namely \(B=[\,U,U\cup A'\,]\).  Thus the total from Case 2 is
   209	\[
   210	1\;+\;\sum_{\substack{U\subseteq S\\U\neq\varnothing}}2^{\,|S\setminus U|}
   211	\;=\;
   212	1\;+\;\sum_{k=1}^n\binom nk\,2^{\,n-k}
   213	\;=\;
   214	1\;+\;\bigl(3^n-2^n\bigr)
   215	\;=\;3^n-2^n+1.
   216	\]
   217	Adding both cases yields in total
   218	\[
   219	2^n\;+\;\bigl(3^n-2^n+1\bigr)
   220	\;=\;3^n+1.
   221	\]
   222	
   223	Answer. \(\displaystyle 3^n+1\) colorings satisfy the required condition.

    13	    ## Problem
    14	
    15	    Let \( s_{1}, s_{2}, s_{3}, \ldots \) be an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers, meaning it is not the case that \( s_{1}=s_{2}=s_{3}=\ldots \). Suppose that \( t_{1}, t_{2}, t_{3}, \ldots \) is also an infinite, nonconstant sequence of rational numbers with the property that \((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\) is an integer for all \( i \) and \( j \). Prove that there exists a rational number \( r \) such that \((s_{i}-s_{j}) r\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j}) / r\) are integers for all \( i \) and \( j \).
    16	
    17	    ## Candidate Solution Attempt
    18	
    19	    Proof.  For any nonzero rational number \(x\) and any prime \(p\), let \(v_{p}(x)\) be the usual \(p\)-adic valuation of \(x\) (so \(v_{p}(x)\in\Bbb Z\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(v_{p}(xy)=v_{p}(x)+v_{p}(y)\), and \(x\) is a \(p\)-adic integer if and only if \(v_{p}(x)\ge0\)).  We will show that the required \(r\) can be chosen so that for every prime \(p\),
    20	\[
    21	v_{p}(r)\;=\;-\,\min_{i,j}v_{p}\!\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr).
    22	\]
    23	Since we will see that \(\min_{i,j}v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\), this prescription makes \(r\)
    24	a well–defined nonzero rational number, and then one checks easily that
    25	\[
    26	v_{p}\!\bigl(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\bigr)
    27	\;=\;
    28	v_{p}(r)+v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})
    29	\;\ge\;
    30	0,
    31	\]
    32	and
    33	\[
    34	v_{p}\!\Bigl(\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}\Bigr)
    35	\;=\;
    36	v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})-v_{p}(r)
    37	\;=\;
    38	v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})+\min_{k,\ell}v_{p}(s_{k}-s_{\ell})
    39	\;\ge\;0,
    40	\]
    41	so that \(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j})/r\) are both integers.  It remains only to check two things:
    42	
    43	1.  For every prime \(p\), the minima
    44	   \[
    45	     a_{p}\;:=\;\min_{i,j}v_{p}\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr),
    46	     \quad
    47	     b_{p}\;:=\;\min_{i,j}v_{p}\bigl(t_{i}-t_{j}\bigr)
    48	   \]
    49	   are finite integers (not \(-\infty\)), that they satisfy
    50	   \(\,a_{p}+b_{p}\ge0\), and that \(a_{p}=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\).
    51	
    52	2.  Defining \(v_{p}(r)=-\,a_{p}\) for each \(p\) indeed gives a rational \(r\) (i.e.\ \(v_{p}(r)=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\)).
    53	
    54	Once these are in hand, the verification that \(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\) and \((t_{i}-t_{j})/r\) are integers is immediate from the additivity of \(v_{p}\).  We now carry out those two steps.
    55	
    56	---
    57	
    58	Step 1.  Bounding the \(p\)-adic minima.  
    59	
    60	Fix a prime \(p\).  Since the sequence \((s_{i})\) is nonconstant, there exist \(i,j\) with \(s_{i}\ne s_{j}\), so \(s_{i}-s_{j}\ne0\) and \(v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})\) is a finite integer.  Hence
    61	\[
    62	  a_{p}
    63	  \;=\;\min_{i,j}v_{p}\bigl(s_{i}-s_{j}\bigr)
    64	  \;>\;-\infty.
    65	\]
    66	Similarly \(b_{p}>-\infty\).  On the other hand by hypothesis
    67	\[
    68	  (s_{i}-s_{j})\,(t_{i}-t_{j})
    69	  \;=\;\text{an integer},
    70	\]
    71	so for every \(i,j\)
    72	\[
    73	  v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})\,+\,v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})
    74	  \;=\;
    75	  v_{p}\!\bigl((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\bigr)
    76	  \;\ge\;0.
    77	\]
    78	Taking the minimum of the left‐hand side over all \(i,j\) gives
    79	\[
    80	  \min_{i,j}\bigl(v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})+v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})\bigr)
    81	  \;\ge\;0
    82	  \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
    83	  a_{p}+b_{p}\;\ge\;0.
    84	\]
    85	It remains to show \(a_{p}=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\).  If \(a_{p}<0\), then \(p\) divides the denominator of some difference \(s_{i}-s_{j}\).  But then \(v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})\ge -\,v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})>0\), so \(p\) divides the numerator of that difference \(t_{i}-t_{j}\).  In particular
    86	\[
    87	  t_{i}\;\equiv\;t_{j}\pmod p
    88	  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    89	  t_{k}\;\equiv\;t_{j}\pmod p
    90	  \quad\text{for all }k,
    91	\]
    92	because \((s_{i}-s_{j})(t_{i}-t_{j})\in\Bbb Z\) for \emph{every} \(i\), \(j\).  Hence \(t_{k}-t_{\ell}\) is divisible by \(p\) for all \(k,\ell\).  But an integer divisible by infinitely many primes must be zero.  Therefore
    93	\[
    94	  \bigl(t_{k}-t_{\ell}\bigr)=0
    95	  \quad\forall\,k,\ell,
    96	\]
    97	contradicting the assumption that \((t_{i})\) is nonconstant.  Thus only finitely many primes \(p\) can satisfy \(a_{p}<0\), and for all the other (indeed almost all) primes \(a_{p}\ge0\), i.e.\ \(a_{p}=0\).
    98	
    99	---
   100	
   101	Step 2.  Defining \(r\) and checking it is rational.  
   102	
   103	We now set
   104	\[
   105	  v_{p}(r)\;=\;-\,a_{p},
   106	  \qquad
   107	  \text{for every prime }p.
   108	\]
   109	Since \(a_{p}=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\), it follows that \(v_{p}(r)=0\) for all but finitely many \(p\), so the product formula in the theory of valuations shows that there is a unique nonzero rational number \(r\) with exactly these \(p\)-adic valuations.  (Concretely, if the “bad” primes \(p\) with \(a_{p}\ne0\) are \(p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\), then one takes
   110	\[
   111	   r\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}^{-\,a_{p_{i}}}
   112	\]
   113	up to an overall choice of sign.)
   114	
   115	---
   116	
   117	Step 3.  Verifying the integrality conditions.  
   118	
   119	Finally, for any indices \(i,j\) and any prime \(p\),
   120	\[
   121	  v_{p}\!\bigl(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\bigr)
   122	  \;=\;
   123	  v_{p}(r)+v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})
   124	  \;=\;-a_{p}+v_{p}(s_{i}-s_{j})
   125	  \;\ge\;-a_{p}+a_{p}
   126	  \;=\;0,
   127	\]
   128	so \(r(s_{i}-s_{j})\) is a \(p\)-adic integer for every \(p\), hence an (ordinary) integer.  Similarly
   129	\[
   130	  v_{p}\!\Bigl(\frac{t_{i}-t_{j}}{r}\Bigr)
   131	  \;=\;
   132	  v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})-v_{p}(r)
   133	  \;=\;
   134	  v_{p}(t_{i}-t_{j})+a_{p}
   135	  \;\ge\;b_{p}+a_{p}
   136	  \;\ge\;0,
   137	\]
   138	so \((t_{i}-t_{j})/r\) is also an integer.  This completes the proof.  ∎
